reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Characteristic lesions are small, firm, dome-shaped papules with a central dimple (umbilication), often pearly or skin-coloured
Spread occurs by direct skin contact, autoinoculation from scratching, and shared items such as towels; in adults, involvement of the genital area can indicate sexual transmission
It is common and typically self-limiting in immunocompetent children, so reassurance and expectant management are often appropriate
A surrounding patch of eczema (molluscum dermatitis) or an inflamed, tender lesion (the beginning-of-the-end sign) often heralds resolution rather than bacterial infection
Extensive, giant, or facial lesions in an adult should prompt consideration of underlying immunosuppression, including HIV

Physical treatments (such as cryotherapy or curettage) and topical agents can be offered when lesions are troublesome, but must be weighed against discomfort and scarring, especially in young children
Advise measures to limit spread: avoid sharing towels, discourage scratching and shaving over lesions, and cover lesions where practical
Reassure that most cases clear spontaneously over months, though this can take a year or more
reference.pathophysiology: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a poxvirus (molluscum contagiosum virus) that replicates within epidermal keratinocytes. The virus induces localised proliferation of the epidermis and produces large intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies (Henderson-Paterson bodies) packed with viral particles, which form the soft core expressed from the umbilicated centre. The virus encodes proteins that dampen the local host immune response, allowing lesions to persist; eventual immune recognition produces the inflammatory reaction that precedes clearance. Transmission is by direct contact, fomites, and autoinoculation, and impaired cell-mediated immunity permits widespread or atypical disease.
additionalDifferentials: Closed comedones or early acne papules
Basal cell carcinoma (for a solitary lesion in an adult)
Disseminated cutaneous cryptococcosis or other opportunistic infections in the immunocompromised
Ectopic sebaceous glands or adnexal tumours
additionalInvestigations: Usually a clinical diagnosis supported by dermoscopy showing central white-yellow structures with surrounding vessels
Consideration of HIV or other immunodeficiency testing when disease is extensive, facial, or atypical in an adult
Screening for other sexually transmitted infections when genital lesions suggest sexual transmission
Biopsy or expression of the core for microscopy in diagnostically uncertain cases
redFlags: Numerous, giant, or facial lesions in an adult suggesting significant immunosuppression such as advanced HIV
A solitary firm nodule in an adult that could represent basal cell carcinoma or an opportunistic infection mimic
Marked periocular involvement risking conjunctivitis or keratitis
reference.prognosis: In immunocompetent individuals the condition is benign and self-limiting, usually resolving spontaneously over several months to a couple of years without scarring; recovery is slower and lesions more extensive when cell-mediated immunity is impaired.
pitfalls: Mistaking the inflamed, resolving lesion for bacterial infection and treating with unnecessary antibiotics
Subjecting young children to painful, scarring procedures for a self-limiting condition
Missing underlying immunosuppression when an adult presents with widespread or atypical lesions
Overlooking sexual transmission and associated infections in adults with genital involvement
